title: The Firefly Night
sum: During a week at Grandma Lou's farm, Nora and her little brother Otis catch fireflies at dusk, learn why they flash, and help them shine by saving the long grass and switching off the barn light.

cast.d: a seven-year-old girl who notices small things and writes them in her notebook
cast.look: a seven-year-old girl with a long brown braid, a green T-shirt, shorts and red rubber boots, holding a small notebook

cast.d: Nora's five-year-old brother, loud, fast and bad at waiting
cast.look: a five-year-old boy with messy blond hair, an orange dinosaur T-shirt and a missing front tooth

cast.d: the children's grandma, who lives on a small farm with hens, a barn and a big back field
cast.look: an older woman with short gray curls, round glasses, a rolled-up denim shirt and muddy boots

cast.d: Grandma Lou's old yellow dog, who sleeps a lot and barks at flashlights
cast.look: a big, sleepy yellow dog with a gray chin and floppy ears

p: Grandma Lou handed Nora an empty pickle jar. It still smelled like pickles. “Tonight we catch fireflies,” she said.
Otis jumped off the porch step. “Now?” “Not yet,” said Grandma. “They come out at dusk, when the sun is gone but the sky isn't black yet.”
Otis ran in to check the kitchen clock. It was only seven o'clock, and dusk wasn't until nine. “Two more hours?” He flopped onto the porch and groaned.
Grandma got a hammer and a nail. Tap, tap, tap! She made six small holes in the lid so the fireflies could breathe. Nora tucked a wet paper towel inside, because fireflies dry out fast.
They ate supper out on the porch swing. Pickles, Grandma's old yellow dog, fell asleep on Otis's feet. “Is it dark yet?” Otis asked. He asked again with his mouth full of corn.
Nora counted his questions on her fingers. Ten fingers were not enough. He asked eleven times! The sky turned orange, then pink, then purple.
Then Nora saw it. A tiny yellow-green light blinked by the fence, and then it was gone. “There!” she whispered.
Otis grabbed the jar and ran to the fence. Pickles woke up and ran right between his legs. Thump! Down went Otis.
“Don't chase the light,” said Grandma. “Watch where it goes. It will blink again, a little higher up.”
Nora stood as still as a post. Blink. Then, a little higher, blink! She held out one finger, and the little light landed on it. Its feet tickled.
By half past nine, Nora had put three fireflies in the jar. Otis put in two. He caught one, and the other landed on his sleeve all by itself!
Up close, a firefly was not a fly at all. It had six legs and two hard wing covers, like a ladybug. “It's a beetle,” said Grandma.
Its light was at the very end of its body. When it blinked, the whole jar glowed green. Nora held the jar to her cheek, but the glow was not warm at all.
“Can I keep one by my bed?” Nora asked. Grandma shook her head. “Fireflies have busy nights. We look, and then we let them go.”
So Nora took off the lid. One light climbed out and floated up into the dark. Another followed, and another.
Otis waved at each one. “Night, bug. Night, bug. Night, bug…”

art.s: On a farmhouse porch at dusk, a seven-year-old girl holds a pickle jar with a few glowing fireflies while her little brother sits in the grass next to a sleepy yellow dog.

q.q: Draw a firefly the way Nora saw it in the jar. Where is its light?
look: two wing covers on its back
a glow at the very end of its body
q.e: You looked as closely as Nora did!

q.q: Grandma said fireflies come out at dusk. What is dusk?
q.a: When the sun is gone, but the sky isn't black yet.
q.e: Dusk is the time between day and night. That's when fireflies start to blink!

q.q: Nora put three fireflies in the jar. Otis put in two. How many were in the jar?
c: 3 fireflies
4 fireflies
5 fireflies
6 fireflies
q.e: Three and two more make five. Five little lights!

p: The next night, Grandma Lou gave each of them a small flashlight. Nora brought her notebook too. Otis stuffed his flashlight in a pocket and grabbed a butterfly net. It was almost as tall as he was.
At nine o'clock, the first lights rose out of the back field. Otis swung his net at every one, whoosh, whoosh, but he did not catch a thing.
Nora did not swing anything. She picked one firefly and watched only that one. It flew low, then flashed as it swooped up. The flash made a little curve, like the letter J.
Then it went dark, and Nora counted in her head. One, two, three, four, five, flash! She counted again, and it flashed again on five.
“It flashes every five seconds,” Nora said. “My turn!” Otis found the same light and stared.
Flash! “Five!” Flash! “Ten!” At every flash, Otis said the next number, all the way up to twenty.
Right after one flash, a tiny light blinked back from the grass below. One, two, blink. That light did not fly. It blinked once and waited.
“Who's that?” Nora whispered. “That's a girl firefly,” said Grandma Lou. “She waits in the grass. The ones flying around are the boys.”
Grandma pointed at the swooping light. “He flashes to ask, ‘Where are you?’ She flashes back, ‘Over here!’”
Otis's mouth fell open. “They're talking?” “With lights instead of words,” said Grandma.
Nora wrote it down in her notebook. Boy: flash, wait five. Girl: count two, flash back. Then she looked down at her flashlight.
She waited for the boy to flash, and then she counted, “One, two.” Click! The firefly turned in the air and flew right down onto her flashlight!
“It thinks I'm a firefly!” Nora said. Otis dropped his net and dug out his flashlight. Click, click, click! He waved it everywhere.
Pickles barked at the beam, but not one firefly came. “You're shouting,” said Nora. “Whisper it. Just once.”
Otis frowned, but he held his flashlight still. When a light swooped up over the grass, he counted, “One, two.” Click.
The firefly turned and floated down, down, down, right onto his thumb. Otis did not move. “It answered me,” he whispered.
The firefly blinked once more on his thumb. Then it flew back to the grass, where a little light was waiting.

art.s: In a dark field, a girl clicks a small flashlight and a firefly swoops down toward it, while her little brother holds a butterfly net taller than he is.

q.q: Otis counted by fives at each flash, up to 20. Draw the flashes in a row. Write his numbers under them.
look: the same space between the flashes
q.e: Five, ten, fifteen, twenty. Four flashes, five seconds apart!

q.q: Why do fireflies flash their lights?
c: to keep warm at night
to find each other
to see where they fly
to scare the dog away
q.e: A boy flashes ‘Where are you?’ and a girl flashes back ‘Over here!’ That's how they find each other.

q.q: Nora told Otis, “You're shouting.” He wasn't using his voice. What did she mean?
q.a: His light was flashing too much, all over the place.
q.e: A firefly answers with one small blink. All that flashing was like yelling!

p: Grandma Lou had a new light high on her barn. It lit up the whole barnyard, almost like daytime. She switched it on every evening when she put the hens to bed. Then she forgot about it until morning.
On Wednesday night, Otis stood under that light with his jar. Moths came. A fat June bug bonked into the light. Not one firefly came.
Down the hill, by the creek, the dark was full of tiny green lights. Nora looked from the barn to the creek and back again. She scrunched up her nose.
Otis tugged her sleeve. “Why are you making that face?” “I'm puzzled,” said Nora. “Why are they all down there?”
“Let's count them,” Nora said. Grandma lent them her kitchen timer. It was shaped like a tomato, and Otis got to hold it.
First they stood by the barn, and Otis turned the tomato to one minute. Tick, tick, tick. Nora counted every light near the barn. When the timer rang, she had only six.
Next they walked down to the creek with Grandma. The grass was wet, and the frogs went quiet. Otis turned the tomato again, and Nora counted as fast as she could.
Otis tried to count too, but at nineteen a firefly landed on his ear. He giggled and lost his place. Ding! Nora's number was much bigger this time.
She wrote both numbers in her notebook: Barn 6, Creek 34. Was it the water? The frogs? Or that big barn light?
Nora sent Otis up the hill to the barn. Then she clicked her flashlight once, down in the dark. “I see it!” Otis yelled.
Now it was Otis's turn. He stood right under the barn light and clicked once, just like Nora. Down at the creek, Nora squinted. She could hardly see it.
Otis ran back down, puffing. “Did you see it?” “Barely,” said Nora. “It got lost in all that light, like a birthday candle in the sunshine.”
Nora looked up at the barn light. “So the fireflies' flashes get lost up there too. They can't find each other!” Grandma rubbed her chin. “But I need that light for the hens.”
So they stayed down by the creek, where it was dark. Otis caught a firefly at last. He let it go right there. It blinked all the way down to a little light in the grass.

art.s: At night, a big light shines on a red barn with almost no fireflies near it, while down the hill by a dark creek a girl counts tiny green lights and her brother holds a tomato-shaped kitchen timer.

q.q: By the creek, Nora counted 34 lights. By the barn, she counted 6. How many more were by the creek?
q.e: 34 take away 6 is 28. The dark creek had lots more!

q.q: Nora said she was puzzled. What does puzzled mean?
c: very sleepy
a bit scared
really excited
not sure why
q.e: Nora didn't know why the fireflies were all at the creek. So she counted to find out!

q.q: Draw the bright barn light and the dark creek. Show where Nora saw more fireflies.
look: a bright light by the barn with only a few fireflies
the dark creek full of fireflies
q.e: Your picture shows it! Fireflies need the dark to see each other's flashes.

p: On Thursday morning, Grandma Lou pulled the mower out of the shed. “The back field is up to my knees,” she said. “Time for a haircut.”
Nora put down her toast. Every night, that long grass was full of blinking fireflies. “Wait,” she said, “where do the fireflies go in the daytime?”
Grandma leaned on the mower. “Let's go and look.” The grass tickled their legs as they walked in.
Otis found one first, hanging very still under a blade of grass. In the daylight, it was just a small brown beetle with its light off.
“It's sleeping,” Otis whispered. Grandma looked at the field. “The mower can wait until tomorrow,” she said. “Tonight we'll see who else lives here.”
That evening, a little rain fell. Afterward, the air smelled like wet dirt. Nora and Otis followed Grandma to the edge of the field and turned off their flashlights.
Otis grabbed Nora's arm. Down on the ground, tiny green lights were glowing. They did not blink like fireflies. They glowed for a while, then faded away.
“The fireflies fell down!” Otis said. Nora knelt in the wet grass to look. The light came from a tiny gray bug that looked like a caterpillar wearing armor.
“A glowworm,” said Grandma. “That's a baby firefly. The babies live in the damp dirt and old leaves for a year or more. Then they grow wings.”
“What do they eat?” asked Otis. “Slugs and snails,” said Grandma. Otis stuck out his tongue. “Yuck. Good job, babies.”
Nora looked around the old log and counted seven glowworms. Otis found five more by the rain barrel. He named every one of them Sparky.
Grandma stood in the dark and looked at all the little lights. “So if I mow this field—” “All their hiding places will be gone,” said Nora.
The next morning, Grandma mowed only the front of the field. She left the back corner long. Nora made a sign from a cereal box and pushed it into the grass.
It said FIREFLY NURSERY, PLEASE DO NOT MOW. “What's a nursery?” Otis asked. “A place for babies,” said Nora. “Like your room when you were tiny.”
Just then, Pickles flopped down in the long grass for a nap. Otis pointed at the sign. “It's for babies!” “He's a very old baby,” said Grandma.

art.s: At night after rain, a girl and her little brother kneel in long wet grass by an old log, looking at tiny green glowworms on the ground while their grandma watches.

q.q: Nora's sign said FIREFLY NURSERY. What is a nursery?
c: a place where mowers are kept
a place where hens lay eggs
a place where babies are cared for
a place where frogs sing at night
q.e: A nursery is a place for babies. The baby fireflies grow up in the long grass!

q.q: What does a glowworm grow up to be?
q.e: A glowworm is a baby firefly. After a year or more in the damp ground, it grows wings.

q.q: Nora found 7 glowworms by the log. Otis found 5 by the rain barrel. Draw them all. How many is that?
q.e: Seven and five make twelve. That's a lot of little lights!

p: It was the last night at Grandma Lou's farm. Tomorrow Mom was coming to take them home. Nora had one more job to do first.
Nora opened her notebook to Wednesday: Barn 6, Creek 34. Then she looked up at the big barn light.
“Grandma, can we turn it off tonight?” Nora asked. Grandma Lou looked over at the coop. “I need it to lock up the hens. They go to bed at dusk, and I close their door at nine.”
Nora chewed her pencil. Hens in bed at nine. Fireflies out after nine. “So the light can go off at nine!”
“But I always forget,” said Grandma. So Nora made a sign in big letters and taped it by the switch. HENS IN? LIGHT OFF!
Otis drew a firefly under the words. It looked a bit like a potato with wings. “Best potato I ever saw,” said Grandma.
At nine o'clock, the hens were on their perch, fluffed up like pillows. Grandma shut the coop door, read the sign and laughed. Click! The barn light went off.
At first, Nora could not see a thing. “Wait,” said Grandma. “Give your eyes a minute.” Little by little, the fence and the grass came back out of the dark.
Then a light flashed over the barnyard. From the grass by the barn door, a tiny light blinked back. Soon there was flash and answer, flash and answer, all around them.
Otis turned Grandma's tomato timer to one minute, and Nora counted. Ding! She wrote 30 in her notebook, right under the 6.
One last time, they caught fireflies in the pickle jar and opened the lid together. The lights floated up past the dark barn. “See you next summer!” Otis called.
“Next summer, some of those glowworms will be flying around the barn too,” said Grandma. “All grown up.” Nora looked over at the tall grass in the back corner.
Down low, under the grass, a tiny green light was glowing. It did not blink. It just glowed, and waited for its turn.

art.s: At night, a grandma and two children stand by a dark barn with a hand-drawn sign by the light switch, while fireflies blink all around the barnyard.

q.q: Make your own sign to help the fireflies. Use four words or fewer, and add a picture.
look: a sign with four words or fewer
words that tell people how to help fireflies
a picture that goes with the words
q.e: Nora's sign had just four words: HENS IN? LIGHT OFF! Short signs are easy to read.

q.q: On Wednesday, Nora counted 6 lights by the barn. Tonight she counted 30. How many more is that?
q.e: 30 take away 6 is 24. Turning off one light made a big difference!

q.q: Why did more fireflies flash by the barn once the light was off?
c: They could see each other's flashes
The air got a lot warmer
The hens were asleep in the coop
The grass there was cut short
q.e: In the dark, every little flash shows up. Now the fireflies could find each other.

fin.q: Nora and Otis helped the fireflies in two ways. One was saving the long grass. What was the other?
fin.a: They made a sign so the barn light went off after the hens were in.
fin.e: The babies kept their long-grass home, and the grown-ups got their dark nights back.

c: They found glowworms by a log
They caught fireflies in a pickle jar
They counted lights by the creek
They turned off the barn light
fin.e: The pickle jar came first. Then the counting, then the glowworms, and last of all, lights out!
